\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38), supporting selective prediction.
Quality estimation does not translate to selection, however: despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, no signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding.
The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) selection fails because instance degeneracy (10\textendash 58\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom despite well-aligned utility; and LP is compressed to near-ineffectiveness (median within-instance range 0.041 nats).
LP selection is inversely associated with degeneracy: at 10\% (Few-NERD), $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 58\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
In the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals (four instance-level, one per-sample log-probability [LP]) for quality estimation and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve strong quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.38), supporting selective prediction.
Quality estimation does not translate to selection, however: despite ${\sim}$13~pp oracle headroom, no signal consistently outperforms greedy decoding.
The gap has a three-layer structure: four instance-level signals cannot rank candidates by construction; Minimum Bayes Risk (MBR) selection fails because instance degeneracy (10\textendash 58\% identical outputs) eliminates headroom despite well-aligned utility; and LP is compressed to near-ineffectiveness (median within-instance range 0.041 nats).
LP selection is inversely associated with degeneracy: at 10\% (Few-NERD), $+1.36$~pp ($p{<}0.001$); at 58\% (CoNLL), LP fails.
In the low-degeneracy regime, LP scales with sample budget ($+0.52$~pp from $N{=}8$ to 16, paired $p{=}0.003$).
Closing the gap for structural signals likely requires learned per-sample scoring.
\end{abstract}
